analysis.one_liner: Restricts how companies and agencies collect, use, and sell COVID-era health and location data.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced during the pandemic with 38 House sponsors, never received a committee hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 pandemic, contact-tracing apps, employers, and data companies began collecting sensitive health information — test results, location histories, who you stood near, even whether you had symptoms. This bill would have required organizations collecting that data to get clear consent, keep it secure, delete it after the emergency ended, and never use it for advertising or to deny someone a job, housing, credit, or the right to vote. It would have given the FTC, state attorneys general, and individuals the power to sue violators — and it would have overridden forced-arbitration clauses that normally block such lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose health, location, or contact-tracing data was collected during the pandemic — especially workers whose employers could otherwise screen them, consumers targeted by ads based on health status, and people whose data might be used against their right to vote. It also protects groups facing discrimination based on health data, and requires government reports on the civil rights impact of pandemic data collection.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose health and location data was collected

how_it_helps.text: Requires any organization collecting COVID-era health data to get affirmative express consent — not buried consent — and to let people revoke it and have their data destroyed within 30 days [S3].

Bans using emergency health data for commercial advertising, for e-commerce recommendations, or to make employment, finance, credit, insurance, housing, or education opportunities unavailable based on health status [S3].

Bars government entities and covered organizations from denying, restricting, or interfering with anyone's right to vote based on their health data or participation in a contact-tracing program, and lets individuals sue to enforce this [S3].

Requires covered organizations holding data on 100,000 or more people to publicly report every 90 days what data they collect and who they share it with, and mandates destruction of all emergency health data 60 days after the emergency ends [S3].

Enforces the rules through the FTC, state attorneys general, and a private right of action with statutory damages of $100 to $5,000 per violation, and declares pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable for claims under the bill [S3].
Directs HHS to report on the civil rights impact of pandemic health-data collection and on policies requiring digital contact-tracing or health-monitoring tools [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect, sell, or monetize health and location data — data brokers, advertising technology firms, employers running screening programs, and developers of contact-tracing and symptom-checking apps — which would face compliance costs, public disclosure requirements, FTC penalties, state lawsuits, and individual suits. Tech platforms that wanted to profit from pandemic-era health data would lose that market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, and app developers

drawbacks.text: Compliance would have been genuinely difficult: the bill required an FTC rulemaking within 45 days of enactment covering data already collected, a compressed timeline that could have produced rushed rules for a fast-moving pandemic response [S3].

The private right of action with statutory damages per violation, combined with a ban on arbitration, could have exposed even good-faith contact-tracing efforts to class-action litigation, which public health officials worried could slow voluntary participation in tracing programs [S3].

Critics of sweeping data-privacy mandates generally argued that rigid, emergency-specific rules risk making contact-tracing tools harder to build and use effectively; the bill excluded health care providers and public health authorities from its main requirements but left app developers fully covered [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits were concrete and timely: in 2020 there was no comprehensive federal privacy law covering the flood of health and location data collected through contact-tracing apps and workplace screening, and health data could legally be used for advertising or to shape access to jobs and housing. The main costs were compliance burdens and litigation risk for tech companies and employers, and some risk that liability fears would chill voluntary contact-tracing participation. The bill tried to manage that risk by exempting health care providers, public health authorities, and manual case investigation, so the tradeoff leaned clearly toward protecting individuals.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the bill on May 14, 2020, during the first months of the pandemic, with five original cosponsors [S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over health and consumer protection [S1].
Thirty-seven additional House Democrats signed on as cosponsors, for a total of 38 sponsors, all Democrats [S4].
The bill's only actions were introduction and committee referral; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in the House before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that collected and profited from pandemic-era health and location data — data brokers, advertising firms, and contact-tracing app developers — kept operating with no federal privacy rules beyond HIPAA, which does not cover most apps or employers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and app developers, still unregulated

sides.party_line_note: All 38 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past its Democratic-controlled committee referral.

industries.industry: Data brokers and advertising technology firms
industries.note: The bill would have banned using emergency health data for commercial advertising and required public reporting of data practices, directly cutting off a market for monetizing pandemic-era health and location information [S3]. Its interest in blocking the bill ran against individuals' control over their own health data.

The bill imposed consent, security, disclosure, and deletion duties on app developers while exempting public health authorities and manual contact tracing [S3]. Developers faced real compliance costs and litigation exposure, though clear federal rules could also have built user trust in tracing apps.
The bill barred using health data to make employment opportunities unavailable and required consent for collecting employee health and location data [S3].
The bill declared pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable for claims under the act, removing a common shield against consumer lawsuits [S3].
